project.description: Static review of the source tree secp256k1 at 1b4181f93f7a53639223ced4c347d0d0d2c2ff9c. 99 files analysed; of 189 files, 37 are test, fuzzing, benchmark or example code and were left out, 53 are not read by any analyzer, 0 exceed the per-file limit and 0 did not fit the total limit. No requests were sent to the owner's systems.

decisions.note: The row that matters more than any other in the portfolio. This is the implementation every audited self-custody wallet reaches in the end: Jade vendors libwally, which vendors this; Krux pins embit, which nests a zkp fork of this; SeedSigner pins embit from PyPI, which binds to this through ctypes; rust-bitcoin reaches it through rust-secp256k1's secp256k1-sys. The anchors are the public surface rather than internals — include/secp256k1.h:75, src/secp256k1.c:20 and :373, src/ecdsa.h and src/ecdsa_impl.h, and the recovery module at src/modules/recovery/main_impl.h:74. Exposure is forward-only for a key never used, and retroactive in the practical sense for any key whose public form is already on chain, which is most of them. A post-quantum signature standard does replace this, by consensus change rather than by a library release — so the library is not where the fix happens, which is exactly why knowing its shape matters.

Correct. include/secp256k1_schnorrsig.h:82, src/modules/schnorrsig/main_impl.h:98 and the MuSig session at src/modules/musig/session_impl.h:583. Taproot and MuSig sit on the same hardness assumption as ECDSA: BIP-340 fixed malleability and enabled aggregation, not quantum resistance. MuSig is worth naming separately because key aggregation publishes an aggregate public key early in the protocol, so a multi-party wallet exposes a key before it is spent from.

The only row in this repository with a *retroactive* character, which is why it should not be read as one more signing row. include/secp256k1_ecdh.h is the key-agreement module, used by BIP-47 payment codes, silent payments and ECIES-style encryption built on top of this library. Where a shared secret derived through it protects stored or recorded data, harvest-now-decrypt-later applies: the ciphertext kept today becomes readable once a CRQC exists, and no later migration undoes that. Unlike the signature rows, that half can be fixed without a consensus change, by wrapping the agreed secret under a hybrid KEM. One row, and the first one anybody building on this library should act on.

Severity dropped to informational, and this is the honest part of the result. Sixteen of the ECDSA rows and one Schnorr row could not be assigned a role because they are not uses: contrib/lax_der_parsing.{c,h} is a DER leniency helper for historical signatures, src/bench*.c and src/modules/schnorrsig/bench_impl.h are benchmarks, src/precompute_ecmult*.c generate static tables at build time, and several hits are the one-line "#include" banner at the top of include/secp256k1_*.h, which names ECDSA because every header in the family does. They are correct inventory — the primitive genuinely appears at those lines — and they are not exposure. Keeping them visible at info rather than deleting them is deliberate: a reader who checks the file list should find the same rows the tool found, and a report that silently drops the uninteresting ones cannot be reproduced.

findings.title: Quantum-vulnerable ECDSA: transaction and message signing (10 file(s))
findings.description: 51 reference(s) to ECDSA across 10 file(s), e.g. include/secp256k1.h:75. Role, judged from paths, function names and nearby code: transaction and message signing. A CRQC derives the private key from a public key that is already known (on chain after the first spend, in reused addresses): funds and approvals controlled by these keys need a migration path.
findings.impact: Long-term risk depends on what the algorithm protects: signatures (authenticity until migration) or key exchange/encryption (retroactive decryption of recorded data).
findings.recommendation: Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them.
findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.
findings.method: Regular-expression matching of crypto API patterns; the role comes from words in paths, enclosing function names and the lines around the matches.

findings.title: Quantum-vulnerable Schnorr (BIP-340): role not determined (1 file(s))
findings.description: 3 reference(s) to Schnorr (BIP-340) across 1 file(s), e.g. src/modules/schnorrsig/bench_impl.h:33. Role, judged from paths, function names and nearby code: role not determined. The code does not show what the keys protect; review decides the priority.
findings.impact: Long-term risk depends on what the algorithm protects: signatures (authenticity until migration) or key exchange/encryption (retroactive decryption of recorded data).
findings.recommendation: Classify each usage, record data lifetimes, and plan migration to a post-quantum algorithm; introduce an abstraction layer for crypto-agility.
findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.
findings.method: Regular-expression matching of crypto API patterns; the role comes from words in paths, enclosing function names and the lines around the matches.
findings.repro: Open src/modules/schnorrsig/bench_impl.h:33 and inspect the quoted lines; the evidence lists further files.

triage.note: Severity dropped to informational, and this is the honest part of the result. Sixteen of the ECDSA rows and one Schnorr row could not be assigned a role because they are not uses: contrib/lax_der_parsing.{c,h} is a DER leniency helper for historical signatures, src/bench*.c and src/modules/schnorrsig/bench_impl.h are benchmarks, src/precompute_ecmult*.c generate static tables at build time, and several hits are the one-line "#include" banner at the top of include/secp256k1_*.h, which names ECDSA because every header in the family does. They are correct inventory — the primitive genuinely appears at those lines — and they are not exposure. Keeping them visible at info rather than deleting them is deliberate: a reader who checks the file list should find the same rows the tool found, and a report that silently drops the uninteresting ones cannot be reproduced.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: 2026 estimates for a 256-bit curve: under 1,200 logical qubits and 90 million Toffoli gates, under half a million physical superconducting qubits running for minutes (Babbush et al.); 1,193 logical qubits with more gates (Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher); P-256 in a few days on 26,000 neutral-atom qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

scenario.rationale: Inside the 10-year horizon the survey puts at 28-49% ('quite possible'), and consistent with the BSI estimate of 15 years that 'could shrink to 10 or even less'. Use it for data that must stay confidential for decades, where being wrong is expensive.
